cards.title: Find a pane by what is in it
cards.notes:
Type `dev`, land in the pane running the dev server, whichever project it belongs to. The picker, but over panes rather than projects. Thirty panes across five projects is the size where a list stops working and a search starts.

fuzzy.ts and the picker overlay are already there, so the work is small. It depends on the naming card: without names there is nothing to match on but `terminal 3`.

Weigh it against the manager page first. If that page already lists every pane by name with Enter to jump, this is the same feature with a filter box on it, and the answer may be to put the filter there rather than build a second way in.

cards.title: Search every open project at once
cards.notes:
One box, ripgrep over every open project's folder, results grouped by project. Enter on a result opens that project's nvim at the line. Today `where did I write that` costs a guess about which project, a tab switch, and a search once you are there.

Spawning ripgrep is the easy half. The results list is the work: grouping, showing the matching line, and what to do about four hundred hits. It also needs ripgrep on the machine, or something slower behind it.

An overlay you open from anywhere, like the picker -- not a corner of the manager page. Searching is something you want from the pane you are in, not somewhere you navigate to first.

What it adds over `rg` in a pane, which already works and which your fingers know, is only the across-projects part. That is worth something with five open and nothing when you already know which one.

cards.title: A project remembers what its panes should be running
cards.notes:
Pane 1 runs the dev server, pane 2 the test watcher, pane 3 claude, stored with the project. The session card put the layout back and left this out on purpose -- same projects, same order, same view, same focused pane, and five empty shells. So every morning the same three commands go into the same three panes by hand.

Sending a command to a pane is plumbing that already exists. The new parts are where the commands are kept and when they fire: on launch, on opening the project, or only when asked.

The question that decides the design is what happens when something is already running. Reopen a project that is already open and `npm run dev` must not go into the pane that is running it -- you get a port already in use, or worse, two of them. Knowing whether a pane is busy is the same thing the send-to-many-panes card needs and does not have.

Only the last bit belongs to the manager page -- start all, stop all, one place to see what is up. The storing and running half stands on its own.

Decided: a command runs only into a fresh pane, never into one that already has something in it. Low for now, nothing runs locally today.

cards.title: Send one command to many panes
cards.notes:
Pick panes across projects, type a command once, and it runs in all of them. `git pull` in five repos for one keystroke. Same plumbing as answering a waiting pane, plus a way to select rows.

The danger is the feature: whatever sends `git pull` to thirty shells sends `rm -rf` to thirty shells. So the selection has to be visible, the confirmation has to name the count, and it should refuse a pane that is not sitting at a prompt -- a pane mid-agent-session takes the command into Claude Code's input box rather than a shell. Knowing which panes are idle needs shell integration we do not have, so decide what to do about that before building the rest.

cards.title: What each pane last printed, and how long ago
cards.notes:
Main sees every byte of every pty. Keep the last non-blank line and the time it arrived, and thirty shells across five projects fit on one screen: `api . terminal 1, 2s ago, 214 tests passed`. The age is the half that earns it -- `quiet 41 minutes` is how you spot the pane you forgot.

The last line is a guess, and the page should not pretend otherwise. Spinners and progress bars redraw one line forever, so the text can be stale in a way the age will not show. Strip the escape codes, take the last line with printable characters in it, and accept it is approximate.

cards.title: A fourth mode: notes, one page of them per project
cards.notes:
A project gets somewhere to write things down that are not a card. Free text, one page, kept with the project rather than on the board: `.dashboard/notes.md` beside board.json, so it commits or is ignored with everything else the dashboard keeps about a project.

It is a mode like the other three, which means it is a row in actions.ts, a fourth entry in the views record, and a fourth Mode in modes.ts -- session.ts checks a restored mode against that same list, so a saved page comes back on the notes screen the way it comes back on the board. Ctrl+T, Ctrl+N and Ctrl+B are taken and Ctrl+N is the obvious letter, so the default binding needs choosing.

Two rules it has to keep. The mode key passes through to the pane once you are already in the mode. And the editor reads event.key for itself, so it needs the isModified guard or a modified key does something in it that it was never meant to.

Ctrl+H is part of the change: a new section with its own blurb saying what the screen is.

It inherits bidi for free: the one rule in index.css covers every element outside a pane, so a page of Persian notes reads correctly the day the mode exists. The editor is a box you type into, so it carries dir="auto" like the other four.

cards.title: Panes name themselves
cards.notes:
`api . dev server` instead of `api . terminal 3`. One small change and everything else reads better: the waiting list, the notification banner, the status bar, and which pane is on which worktree.

Mostly automatic, from three sources, best first:

1. The program names itself. A terminal title is an escape sequence any program can print -- `printf '\033]0;dev server\007'` -- and xterm.js already parses it and fires an event nobody listens to. Shells set it on every prompt. Claude Code can be told to set it to whatever it is working on, from a line in the project's CLAUDE.md, and then the pane says so while it works.
2. The command it was started with. When the startup commands put `npm run dev` in pane 2, the name is already known.
3. A name you typed, which beats both -- otherwise the next prompt wipes it.

A title is a hint, not a label: shells rewrite it on every command, so taken blindly the name flickers with every `ls`. Take it only when nothing better is set.

`paneLabel` is already the one place a pane's name is spelled and every other part of the app reads it from there, so this is that function preferring a stored name. An unnamed pane still says `terminal 3` -- lose the numbering and the focus keys stop making sense.

cards.title: Read a project's file in a view that does bidi
cards.notes:
Persian prose cannot be read in a pane and never will be, so the way to read a Persian roadmap or README is a screen the app draws itself -- Chromium lays it out correctly there, and the one rule in index.css already covers every element outside a pane.

The open question the design turns on is how the file is chosen: a picker over the project's folder, or whatever file nvim currently has open.

Keyboard-first, so it is a row in actions.ts and a section in help.ts.

Related: the notes mode card is this same screen for a file the app owns. This one is for a file the project owns.

cards.title: macOS may take Ctrl+1..9 for Mission Control, the keys that jump between tabs
cards.notes:
src/actions.ts, the project-jump rows ship Ctrl+1..Ctrl+9 on the mac side. Mission Control's Switch to Desktop 1..9 are the same keys and come alive once you have a second Space. Where they are alive, Ctrl+2 slides you to another desktop instead of jumping to tab 2 - and project-jump is the most-pressed row in the table.

Same shape as the bug PR #23 fixed for Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down, which macOS took for Mission Control and Application windows. That PR wrote the rule down above the table: Ctrl with an arrow belongs to macOS. Ctrl with a digit was not checked.

Not confirmed. First step is ten seconds in System Settings > Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts > Mission Control on a machine with two Spaces. Ctrl+Shift+1..9 for project-move looks clear either way.

If it is real, the fix is not the swap made for the arrows: Cmd+1..Cmd+9 is already terminal-focus on the mac side, so this needs a different family. actions.test.ts already refuses two actions on one key per screen, so a bad swap fails there rather than shipping.

https://github.com/naeemba/dashboard/issues/25
https://github.com/naeemba/dashboard/pull/23

cards.title: Agent state per pane from Claude Code hooks, answered from the manager list
cards.notes: A hook script posts permission_prompt, idle_prompt, agent_needs_input and agent_completed to the app. Main keeps a state per pane, keyed by an environment variable the app sets at spawn. The manager row shows the state and the question text; a key on the row sends the answer to that pane. Bell detection stays as the fallback for shells that are not Claude Code.

cards.title: Pull request status on the Ship card, found from the branch through gh
cards.notes: For each card with a branch and no pull request number, gh pr list --head <branch> finds the number and stores it on the card. For each card with a number, poll gh pr view (state, mergeable, checks, review decision) about once a minute and show one glyph on the card: checks running, checks failed, approved, mergeable, merged. A merged pull request is recorded on the card and never polled again. Open: whether a merged pull request moves the card to Done by itself or only marks it.

cards.title: Move a card on the board with the mouse
cards.notes: Drag a card between columns and within a column with the mouse, doing what Shift+Arrow does from the keyboard. The drag moves the selection to that card first, so the highlight and the pointer name the same row.

cards.title: Discard a card's worktree in one key
cards.notes: On a card in Ship or Doing, one key removes its worktree, deletes the branch, and moves the card back to Todo, after a confirmation like delete. Refuses when the worktree has uncommitted changes, saying so; force needs a second confirmation. Open: whether a pane still running in that worktree blocks the discard or is killed first.

cards.title: Search a pane's scrollback
cards.notes: Cmd+F on macOS opens a small search box at the top of the focused pane; Enter and Shift+Enter jump between matches, Escape closes. Uses the xterm.js search addon. The box gets dir=auto, the key is a row in the actions table, and the help dialog gets the row. Cmd rather than Ctrl because Ctrl+F is the shell's forward-char.

cards.title: Zoom the focused pane to fill the page, and back, like tmux
cards.notes: Option+F makes the focused pane take the whole terminals grid; pressing it again puts it back in place. Same as tmux prefix+z. The key is a row in the actions table and the help dialog gets the row.

cards.title: Review a card's worktree diff in tig
cards.notes: On a card that has a worktree, one key spawns tig <base>..<branch> in the lowest free pane with the worktree as its working directory, reusing the ship's pane picking. tig comes from Homebrew, so the spawn goes through the login shell like nvim. If no pane is free the key refuses and says so, the same way ship does.

cards.title: Main broadcasts worktree changes so the renderer stops polling worktrees.json
cards.notes: Every write to the worktree record in main sends worktree:changed with the new record; the board view and the manager's stacked boards redraw from it instead of reading worktrees.json for themselves. Fixes the card that keeps showing a branch whose worktree was removed. Discarding a worktree and opening tig in one both change worktrees and need this to be seen at once.

cards.title: A command line for the board, so agents can work it
cards.notes: A CLI shipped with the app that edits a project's .dashboard/board.json the same way the app does: create a card, move a card between columns, set the pull request number and branch, set priority, list cards. The ship agent's prompt tells it to move its own card to Done with the pull request number once the pull request is open, so nobody moves cards by hand. Two writers on one file means the app needs a watcher on board.json so a card moved by an agent shows up without re-entering the board.

cards.title: Token usage per project: this five-hour window, this week, and all time
cards.notes: Read Claude Code's session logs under ~/.claude/projects (JSONL; each line has usage counts, model, timestamp and cwd). Group by cwd to get per-project totals. Five-hour window is the rolling sum of the last five hours. Week is the sum since the last weekly reset, whose weekday and hour you set once in settings because the logs do not record it. Shown as a manager page section, one row per project with the three numbers, plus the current five-hour figure in the status bar. Tokens only, no dollars: a price table goes stale. Read-only and offline. The log format is Claude Code's own and may shift under an update.

cards.title: Open the focused pane's scrollback in nvim
cards.notes: One key writes the focused pane's whole buffer to a temp file and opens it in the nvim slot, so an agent transcript can be searched, read and yanked with real editor tools. The key is a row in the actions table and the help dialog gets the row.

cards.title: Remove a project from the open projects
cards.notes: A key on the manager list closes the selected project: its page and five shells go away and it leaves the session. Refuse, and say so, while a pane in it is still running something.

cards.title: Add a manager page as the first tab, giving an overview across projects
cards.notes: A manager for the dashboard app itself, distinct from the other projects. It sits as the first tab, like every other project, but instead of five shells it shows an overview: what is happening, what is waiting on us, everything. What exactly goes on it still needs discussion and review.

cards.title: Run a task across projects and collect the results
cards.notes:
Shipped. The manager page has a strip of three named sections along the top — general, board, command — walked by Alt+H and Alt+L from any of them. Behind the third: type one shell command, mark which open projects it runs in with Space, press Enter, and read one row per project saying how it exited and what it last printed. Enter on a finished row opens its last five lines; Escape stops a run.

Main spawns one process per project through the user's shell with -lic, the same PATH reasoning the editor and agent panes already use. It is not a pty and borrows no pane, so a command asked of five projects never touches what is in your shells.

An action's scope gained one non-mode value, manager-page, meaning any section of the manager. The strip keys have to be heard on all three sections and `board` is a mode every project also has, so `hears` now takes whether the page is the manager. `scopesOverlap` is exported for the settings screen's clash warning, so the key matcher and the warning cannot drift. The help dialog takes the same flag, or it would list the strip keys on a project's own board where they are never heard.

Known cost: renderer.ts is at 570 code lines against the 600 ceiling. The next feature touching it needs the file split first — its own card.

Not doing, deliberately: named tasks saved in settings.json (you type the command, it lasts the session), results surviving a restart, and any history of runs.

https://github.com/naeemba/dashboard/pull/28

cards.title: Start a card in its own worktree, in one of the project's panes
cards.notes:
A key on a card in Doing makes a git worktree and a branch for it, and puts one of the project's five panes into that worktree. You work the card there while the other panes stay on the main checkout. No stashing, and two cards can be in flight at once without standing on each other.

Not a project tab of its own: that would mean a second entry in the session, a second row in the tab strip and a second install of everything, for a checkout that lives a few days.

The pane has to say which branch it is on. Five panes that all read `terminal 3` with two of them in worktrees is how a command lands in the wrong checkout. That is the naming card, and this needs it.

Decide how a pane is pointed at the worktree. Sending it `cd` keeps whatever was in the pane and leaves its shell where the project started; restarting it there is cleaner and throws away the scrollback. Also decide which pane -- picked by you, or a free one, and nothing yet knows which panes are free.

The lifecycle is the work, not the git command. When is the worktree removed, what happens with uncommitted changes in it, what happens when the branch merges, and what stops fifteen stale checkouts collecting on disk. The nvim pane stays on the main checkout unless something says otherwise.

Design agreed 2026-09-10. Ship is a new column between Todo and Doing; moving a card there creates the worktree off a freshly fetched base branch, takes a pane you have never typed in, and starts `claude "/work-card <id>"` in it. In-flight state lives on the branch, never on main; a local worktrees.json in userData carries the badge, the pane label and the cleanup list. Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-10-ship-a-card-into-a-worktree-design.md

Shipped in #27. Ship is a new column second from the left: moving a card there makes a worktree beside the project off a freshly fetched base branch, commits the card's move on that branch, and starts an agent in a pane you have never typed into. A local worktrees.json carries the card's badge, the pane's branch label and the Ctrl+Shift+W list, which is the only place a worktree is ever removed. The agent's own instructions live in dotfiles as /work-card and land separately.

cards.title: Manager tab: a board of every open project, editable in place
cards.notes:
Shipped. Ctrl+B on the manager stacks one board per open project under project headings, and the cards are edited where they sit. Cmd+Up and Cmd+Down on macOS, Ctrl elsewhere, say which project the keys are aimed at — macOS takes Ctrl with an arrow for Mission Control before the app is told, Escape goes back to the pane list.

Not a second board: createBoardView once per project, so every editing key already worked, each project keeps its own undo and writes its own file, and the renderer gained no branch — the view hands back a BoardView, so it sits in the same field and shows in the same mode. The manager page has two views now instead of one. Both screens re-read on arrival and loadBoard clears undo on every read, so neither can undo over the other.

isProjectPage stopped reading the mode. It answered "is this the manager?" with mode !== "manager", and a manager that can sit in board mode counted as a project — saved to the session file, listed in its own waiting list, draggable along the tab strip. It reads the slot, which is the thing about the manager that never moves.

Two rules that were written twice are written once now. heldIndex in clamp-index.ts is how a selection survives the list under it being rebuilt, asked by the manager’s rows and by the boards on its board. SELECTED_CARD is exported from board-view.ts, so the name of the card the keys are on cannot be renamed there and left behind here — nothing would have failed, the selection would just have stopped being scrolled to.

Seeding .dashboard walks its files unconditionally and checks each one on its own, so a folder cloned without its docs gets them back. It runs in front of every read, and this page reads every open project at once, on the process that also pumps the panes.

Known cost: on a project’s own board Ctrl+H lists the three new keys and pressing them there does nothing. Their descriptions say "on the manager". A mode of its own is the only way out, and costs more in MODES, MODE_NAMES, BLURBS, modeLabel and focusMode for the same screen.

No filtering and no file watching — every column and every card, and a card an agent writes while you are looking turns up when you come back. PR #23.

cards.title: A saved settings.json freezes every shipped default
cards.notes:
Shipped in PR #26. writeSettings wrote the whole Settings object, so the first time you nudged a font size, every shipped key and every shipped colour went into ~/.config/dashboard/settings.json as if you had picked it — and parseSettings read them back as your choices forever after.

What it cost: PR #23 moves the manager board's project keys to Cmd+Up / Cmd+Down on macOS, because the system takes Ctrl with an arrow for Mission Control. Anyone who had ever set a font size kept Ctrl+Up. The only way out was deleting the settings file, which took the font and the colours with it.

chosenSettings now leaves out anything equal to what this build ships — keys, theme, font and shellCommand, not just the keys the bug was found through — which is what parseSettings has always assumed a missing line means. An explicit null key stays: it means no key at all.

It also gives `written` its meaning back. A file naming every action made every line written, so the written-first sort in withoutDuplicates settled nothing and ACTIONS row order decided who lost a clashing key.

https://github.com/naeemba/dashboard/pull/26
https://github.com/naeemba/dashboard/issues/24

cards.title: Show a waiting pane's tail, and answer it with a keystroke
cards.notes:
Shipped. A waiting row on the manager carries the last five lines that pane has on screen, and a character typed on that row goes straight to its pty — three agents asking at once are cleared without switching tabs. Five lines, not one: an agent asks with a numbered menu whose options move around. The bell comes off as the key goes out, so the row leaving the list is the sign it landed.

Enter still takes you to the pane; keys with names never reach the pty, since the window's lookup claims them first and a word typed at a pane that has stopped asking is a command the shell runs. A dead pane takes no keys — it wants Enter in the pane. tailLines and takesAnswer are the rules, in manager.ts with tests; isBareCharacter went beside isModified in shortcuts.ts, because whether a keystroke is a typed character is a keyboard question; reading the xterm buffer stayed in renderer.ts as wiring, off the live screen rather than the scrollback. help.ts has the blurb and an `Any single key` row, and the keys no binding names are one table now, shared with nvim's.

Known edge: a capital needs Shift, and Shift is a modifier, so `Y` cannot be sent. Digits and lowercase can. PR #22.

cards.title: Persian typing in a pane was checked and is fine
cards.notes:
Nothing to fix, written down so nobody investigates it twice. macOS's Persian-ISIRI 2901 layout puts ZWNJ -- the نیم‌فاصله, the one character Persian typing cannot do without -- on Shift+Space, and also on Shift+B. Neither is bound to anything in this app, so both reach the pane.

What does sit on Option is ى, ٱ, two diacritics, and the Persian digits ۰-۹ on the numeric keypad. Those are the ones macOptionIsMeta turns into Esc+key, so they cannot be typed into a pane. None of them is standard Persian orthography and a laptop has no keypad, so macOptionIsMeta stays as it is -- turning it off would cost <A-l> in nvim, which is the reason it was set.

Asked of macOS itself through UCKeyTranslate over every keycode and modifier combination, on 2026-09-09, rather than guessed at.

cards.title: Right-to-left text: fixed everywhere the app draws it, never in a pane
cards.notes:
Reproduced, and it splits in two. The app's own text is fixed. A pane cannot be.

What was wrong where we draw it: nothing in the app ever asked for bidi, so a Persian note ending in a full stop drew the stop at the far left of the line and the sentence read as though it began with a period. One rule now asks -- `body *:not(.pane, .pane *) { unicode-bidi: plaintext }` in index.css. Every element rather than a list of the ones holding typed text, because unicode-bidi does not inherit; the list version was written first and already missed the title bar, the column headings, the settings row, the card detail's column names, the branch line and the Directory-not-found path, and would have missed the notes page next. Order only, so the columns still line up; the four boxes you type into carry dir="auto", which turns the box round as well. The manager's arrow became a span of its own -- sharing the name's span it crossed to the far side of a Persian name and stopped lining up with the row above.

What cannot be fixed: anything inside a pane. xterm.js lays out a grid of cells and reorders nothing, and nvim does not do bidi either -- `:help rileft` says so outright. Writing the algorithm into the grid ourselves is the trap: once screen column 5 is no longer buffer cell 5, the cursor, the selection and the mouse all lie, and you click a word and land four characters away. Not worth reopening. `:set rightleft` only helps a file with no English in it, and the webgl renderer's character joiner would leave the cursor wrong regardless.

So Persian prose belongs on a screen the app draws, not in a pane. That is an argument for the notes mode card, and a card worth writing for reading a project's file in a bidi view. PR #21.

Three ways of fixing it inside a pane were tried and none of them works. Written down so the next person does not spend the afternoon again.

1. A bidi filter in front of the pane -- fribidi, which is the Unicode algorithm as a command line tool and is one brew install away. It reorders the text before the terminal sees it. It fights whatever reordering is already going on, and the two together are a different kind of wrong rather than a fix. Also useless for nvim by construction: nvim addresses the cursor per cell, so a filter in the pipe has no line to reorder.
2. xterm.js's character joiner on the webgl renderer, which is the one API that hands several cells to the text shaper as a single run. Loaded the addon, registered a joiner over every right-to-left run, and the output was identical to the default renderer's. It merges draw calls; it does not change the base direction, and the base direction is what puts the words in the wrong order.
3. An option somewhere in xterm.js. There is none: grep the v6 typings for bidi, rtl and direction and there are no hits.

So the only version that could work is bidi in our own renderer -- reorder each row for display and keep a map between visual and logical columns so the cursor, the selection and the mouse stay honest. That map is the whole job. Without it you put the cursor at the start of a Persian word in nvim, press x, and the character that disappears is from the other end of the word. And nvim would still be half wrong, because nvim does its own layout in logical columns -- where the line wraps, where a table column starts -- so reordering the display leaves nvim's idea of the line and what you see disagreeing.

If it is ever wanted, the narrow version is the one to attempt: display-order reordering only, read-only, behind a setting that is off by default. Good enough for cat, bat, less and an agent's output; explicitly not for nvim. Days of work, and it may come out worse than the honest breakage we have. Not chosen.

cards.title: The waiting list, and Enter jumps to the pane
cards.notes: Shipped. Every pane asking for you, named under its project on the manager page, with Enter landing you in it. goToPane is one function now, shared with the notification click, so the two ways into a pane from elsewhere cannot land differently. isRinging moved to waiting.ts and both the tab strip and this list ask it — before, the rule was written twice and dropping `notified` from one would have stopped the tab going yellow while the manager still listed the pane. PR #18.

cards.title: Say which panes have died
cards.notes: Shipped. A pane that exits now shows up on the manager page as `terminal 1 · exited`, red, and Enter on that row takes you to it to press Enter again. The exited flag has always existed and nothing ever read it; onExit redraws now, which is the whole of what was missing. Dead beats asking: a shell that rings on its way out is listed as exited, not waiting, because answering it finds nothing to answer. The tab does not go yellow for a dead pane — yellow means asking today, and giving it a second meaning is a change to the terminals screen, not this page. PR #18.

cards.title: One row per project, and the lists live inside it
cards.notes: Shipped. One row per open project carrying what its panes want — `dashboard · 2 waiting · 1 exited`, or `quiet`. Enter opens a project to name those panes, Enter on a pane lands you there: right tab, right view, keyboard in the pane, and the bell clears on arrival as it always did. Up and Down walk the flat list. The rules are in manager.ts beside a test — managerRows, alertSummary, managerLines, canOpen, selectedLine — and the DOM is in manager-view.ts, the split board.ts and board-view.ts already have. canOpen is the one place deciding a quiet project cannot expand, so the arrow, the drawn lines and the key cannot disagree. The selection is held as what it is on rather than where it is, so a pane that starts asking pushes the highlight along instead of sliding it onto a different pane. Three ordinary rows in the action table under a new manager scope, so they rebind and the help dialog and settings screen print them untold. No age on the row yet — that needs a per-second redraw and belongs with the last-line card. PR #18.

cards.title: A first tab that is not a project
cards.notes: Shipped. The manager sits at the front of the tab strip where a project sits, with no folder, no five shells, no editor and no board. Ctrl+1 lands on it, Ctrl+O comes back to it, a launch with nothing saved opens on it, and nothing can be dragged in front of it. `manager` is a fourth Mode no key selects, and that one fact carries the change: setMode refuses a view the page does not have, which replaces the dead-project check it used to make, and isProjectPage reads the mode so the session file, the picker, the tab drag and the launch landing all ask one question instead of four. Page.views is a Partial record — three views, one, or none. Not written to session.json, and the empty path is a second lock since parseSession already drops a page with no path. The empty window is gone: that state is the manager, and the sentence saying how to open a project moved to its status bar, reading the key and the wording off the action table. Ctrl+H has its own section for it. Nothing is on the page yet — the lists are their own cards. PR #17.

cards.title: Cards remember when they were made and when they last changed
cards.notes: Shipped. A card carries `createdAt` and `updatedAt`, both ISO, both absent rather than null when nobody knows — a board written before the fields existed reads as unknown and stays that way, and nothing is written for a field a card does not have. `updatedAt` moves in editCard, the one funnel every field change goes through, so renaming one card does not stamp the other thirty. A move to another column ages the card; reordering a column does not. Format documented in .dashboard/CLAUDE.md and the copy in board-store.ts, pinned together by the existing test. PR #16.

cards.title: A card knows its branch and its pull request
cards.notes: Shipped. `branch` and `pullRequest` on a card, typed in with `b` and `r`, shown under the card's title so a Doing column says which of its cards is in flight. The number is a whole number above zero written with or without the `#`; isPullRequestNumber decides that for the file parser and for pullRequestFrom, which the commit and the message explaining the refusal both call. flightParts is the one place that says how the pair reads. Nothing fetches them. PR #16.

cards.title: Fix "Open a new project..." doing nothing in the Ctrl+S picker
cards.notes: Hit Ctrl+S, click "Open a new project...", and the folder dialog opens. Confirmed by hand on 2026-09-07 in a build carrying PR #14. There was never a second cause: the quit question was asked with showMessageBoxSync, which stopped the whole main process, so a folder panel already open could never finish. PR #14 asks it with the async showMessageBox and the panel comes back. No code of its own.

cards.title: Stop the open-folder sheet deadlocking against the Quit confirm
cards.notes: The quit question was asked with showMessageBoxSync, which stops the whole main process until it is answered. A folder panel already open could never finish, so projects:open never replied and the renderer showed "reply was never sent". Measured: the main process sat dead for 4.3 seconds in a stripped-down copy of the window. It now asks with the async showMessageBox: the close is always stopped, and answering Quit calls destroy(), which raises no close to answer again. A second close request while the question is up is ignored instead of stacking another question. PR #14.

cards.title: Notify when something in a pane is waiting on us
cards.notes: Out of the app: a system notification when something needs attention, like a Claude session waiting on an answer. In the app: a small in-app notification, and highlight the tab that is waiting. Shipped: the packaged app is re-signed ad hoc so macOS registers it with Notification Center under the same name as its Info.plist, the banner is raised from main instead of the renderer, and a waiting project gets a pulsing red dot on its tab that stops pulsing under reduced motion. PR #13.

cards.title: A settings screen, with the keyboard shortcuts in it
cards.notes: Every key, the theme, the font and the shell live in ~/.config/dashboard/settings.json, and Ctrl+, edits them from the keyboard. One table in actions.ts names every action once; the handler, the help dialog and the settings screen all read it, so a shortcut is no longer written out in three places. A binding is a string like Ctrl+Shift+K and matches the physical key, so Option+H is Option+H whatever character the keyboard reported. Delete the file and everything is back to how it shipped.

cards.title: Give board cards subtasks
cards.notes: Any card can name another as its parent. A subtask is an ordinary card with its own column, priority and subtasks. Tab attaches, Shift+Tab detaches, o opens a card to see and add its children, and a parent shows a bar of where its subtasks have got to.

cards.title: Ctrl+H opens help for the screen you are on
cards.notes: Ctrl+H pops up a dialog listing the shortcuts for the screen you are on: the terminal grid, nvim and the board each have their own set. PR #9.

cards.title: Give the editor pane the PATH the terminals already have
cards.notes: Ctrl+N only ever showed [exited 1]. The pane spawned nvim by name, and an app launched from the Dock has no Homebrew on PATH. nvim now runs through a login shell. PR #8.

cards.title: Ask before closing the window
cards.notes: Closing killed every shell on every page, including anything still running. The window asks first, with Cancel as the default. PR #8.

cards.title: Open on the projects the last run was left on
cards.notes: The layout is saved to session.json and read back at startup: same projects, same order, same view, same focused pane. The shells still start empty. PR #8.

cards.title: Give board cards a priority
cards.notes: urgent, high, medium or low. p cycles it, a colour down the card's left edge shows it, the status bar names it, and s sorts the column urgent first. Sorting is stable, so Shift+up and Shift+down still hold within a priority.

cards.title: Give board cards a description
cards.notes: e opens the card's notes in a textarea. Enter is a newline, Escape commits. The description shows on the card, dimmed, under the title.

cards.title: Clicking a notification takes you to the pane that rang
cards.notes:
The banner says `api . terminal 3 is waiting`, you click it, and the app comes forward on that project with that pane focused. Today the click brings the app up and then you go and find the pane yourself, which is the part the banner was supposed to save you.

Shipped: the pane's id travels with the notification, main hangs a click handler on it, and the renderer sets the view and the focused pane before showing the page. A slot whose project has since been closed is nowhere to go. paneFromId and modeOfPane moved into terminals.ts with tests. PR #15.

cards.title: One clamp, not three: board.ts, board-detail.ts and manager.ts each hold a copy
cards.notes: Shipped. src/clamp-index.ts holds one clampIndex(value, lastIndex) beside one test, and every list in the app reads it: board.ts, board-detail.ts (both the redraw and the arrow keys), manager.ts, manager-view.ts, picker.ts and board-state.ts. The three copies the issue named plus three more found on the way - picker.ts and board-state.ts were the same shape as the others and now read the same, and the card detail dialog wrote the two halves by hand a hundred lines below the copy it shared. The guards that only fed the old clamp are gone too: lastRow and deleteCard no longer floor a number their callers already floor. The “lists here do not wrap” sentence moved onto move() in manager-view.ts, which decides it. Issue: https://github.com/naeemba/dashboard/issues/19 PR: https://github.com/naeemba/dashboard/pull/20
